Q0429

“It is impossible to live pleasantly without living wisely, finely, and justly.” — Epicurus (Letter to Menoeceus)

Verified English quotation. Primary source: Letter to Menoeceus. Theme: life.

Source and attribution

The archive attributes this English wording to Letter to Menoeceus and files it under Epicureanism. That locator distinguishes the passage from loose internet attributions: readers can return to the named work or section to check translation, surrounding argument, and edition-specific wording.

About Epicurus

Epicurus (341–270 BCE) founded the Garden school in Athens, teaching atomist physics and a therapy of desire aimed at ataraxia. He admitted women and slaves as students and wrote extensively; most works are lost, leaving letters and maxims plus Lucretius’s later poem.

How to read this passage

Life is both a biological fact and a practical project. Philosophers debate flourishing, suffering, mortality, and the standards by which a biography can be judged successful or wasted. This passage enters that discussion through life, wisdom, justice.

Concepts in this quote

Life
Philosophy quotes about life ask what makes a life good, meaningful, or worth examining—questions that drive ethics, religion, and everyday decision.
Wisdom
Wisdom is practical insight under uncertainty: knowing what matters, what one does not know, and how to act without false certainty.
Justice
Justice concerns fairness, rights, desert, and the arrangement of institutions that claim to treat people as equals.
